articles.title: Understanding your period
articles.summary: What a period is, how long a normal cycle lasts, and what you can use during your period.
body: A period is the part of the monthly cycle when blood comes out of the vagina for a few days. It is a normal part of a healthy body.

Most periods come about every 28 days, but anywhere from every 21 to 35 days is common. Bleeding usually lasts 2 to 7 days, often about 5, and is heaviest in the first 2 days. The blood is red on heavy days and can be pink or brown on lighter days.
Periods usually start around age 12, but starting earlier or later is common and not usually a worry. For most girls, periods become regular by about age 16 to 18.
Before a period some people feel bloated, have sore breasts, mood changes, spots or headaches. This usually gets better when the period starts. Not everyone gets these feelings.
You can use pads (including washable, reusable pads), tampons, menstrual cups or period underwear. A tampon that is put in correctly should not be felt, and it cannot get lost inside the body.
keyPoints: A cycle of 21 to 35 days is common.
Bleeding for 2 to 7 days is common.
Periods often start around age 12 and become regular by 16 to 18.
whenToGetHelp: Bleeding between periods, after sex, or after your periods have stopped for good (menopause).
Missing three periods in a row when you are not pregnant.
Any big change in your periods that worries you.

faqs.q: What is a period?
faqs.a: A period is when blood comes out of the vagina for a few days as part of the monthly cycle. It is a normal sign that the body is working as expected.

faqs.q: How long is a normal menstrual cycle?
faqs.tags: cycle length regular how often period come days
faqs.a: Most periods come about every 28 days, but every 21 to 35 days is common. Bleeding usually lasts 2 to 7 days, and is heaviest in the first 2 days.

faqs.q: At what age do periods start?
faqs.tags: first period age girl puberty start late early
faqs.a: Periods usually start around age 12. Starting a little earlier or later is common and is not usually a worry. Most girls have regular periods by about 16 to 18.

faqs.q: What can I use during my period?
faqs.tags: pads tampons cup period products hygiene sanitary
faqs.a: You can use pads (including washable, reusable pads), tampons, menstrual cups or period underwear. Choose what is comfortable and available to you. A tampon cannot get lost inside the body.

faqs.q: When should I see a health worker about my periods?
faqs.tags: worry problem irregular missed period bleeding between
faqs.a: See a health worker if you bleed between periods or after sex, if you bleed after your periods have stopped for good, or if you have missed three periods in a row and are not pregnant.

articles.title: Period pain
articles.summary: Why periods can hurt, what you can do at home, and when pain needs a health worker.
body: Period pain is common. It happens because the womb tightens during a period. It is often felt as cramps in the lower tummy that can spread to the back and thighs, and it usually lasts up to 3 days.

Things that can help at home include a warm bath or shower, a hot water bottle wrapped in a cloth on your tummy, gently rubbing your tummy and back, and gentle exercise such as walking. Cutting down on alcohol and not smoking may also help.
Sometimes painful periods are caused by a health condition, such as endometriosis, fibroids or an infection in the pelvis. A coil (IUD) can also cause pain in the first months after it is fitted.
HerHealth does not recommend medicines or doses. A health worker or pharmacist can advise you on what is safe for you.
keyPoints: Period pain is often normal.
Warmth, gentle massage and gentle exercise can help.
Pain that stops your daily life should be checked.
whenToGetHelp: Pain that is severe, worse than usual, or not helped by the things you usually do.
Pain that stops you from doing your normal daily activities.
Periods that become more painful, heavier or irregular.
Pain during sex, or when you pee or poo, or bleeding between periods.
A swollen tummy, loss of appetite, or losing weight without trying.

faqs.q: Is period pain normal?
faqs.a: Some period pain is common. It happens because the womb tightens during your period, and it usually lasts up to 3 days. Pain that is severe, getting worse, or stops your normal daily life should be checked by a health worker.

faqs.q: What can I do at home for period pain?
faqs.tags: relief help cramps remedy home ease
faqs.a: A warm bath or shower, a hot water bottle wrapped in a cloth on your tummy, gently rubbing your tummy and back, and gentle exercise such as walking can help. Cutting down on alcohol and not smoking may also help.

faqs.q: When is period pain a sign of a problem?
faqs.a: Get help if the pain is severe or worse than usual, stops your daily activities, or comes with heavier or irregular periods, pain during sex or when you pee or poo, bleeding between periods, a swollen tummy or weight loss.

articles.title: Heavy periods
articles.summary: How to tell if your periods are heavy, what can cause it, and when to get checked.
body: Many women have heavy periods, and for some this is normal. But if heavy bleeding affects your daily life, a health worker can help.

Signs of heavy periods include needing to change a pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours, needing to use two products at once, bleeding for more than 7 days, passing blood clots bigger than about 2.5 cm, bleeding through to clothes or bedding, or often feeling tired or short of breath.

Heavy periods can happen when periods first start, after pregnancy, or as a woman gets close to menopause. They can also be caused by conditions of the womb or ovaries, bleeding disorders, or some medicines. Rarely, they can be a sign of cancer of the womb.
A health worker may do blood tests, for example to check for a low blood count (anaemia).
keyPoints: Changing a pad every 1 to 2 hours is a sign of heavy bleeding.
Periods lasting more than 7 days should be checked.
Feeling very tired or short of breath can be linked to heavy periods.
whenToGetHelp: Heavy periods that affect your life, or that you have had for some time.
Severe pain during periods.
Bleeding between periods or after sex.

faqs.q: How do I know if my period is too heavy?
faqs.tags: heavy flow lot of blood clots change pad often
faqs.a: Signs include changing a pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours, using two products at once, bleeding for more than 7 days, clots bigger than about 2.5 cm, bleeding through clothes, or often feeling tired or short of breath.

faqs.q: What causes heavy periods?
faqs.a: Heavy periods can happen when periods first start, after pregnancy, or near menopause. They can also be caused by conditions of the womb or ovaries, bleeding disorders or some medicines. Rarely, they can be a sign of womb cancer, so ongoing heavy periods should be checked.

articles.title: Antenatal care: check-ups during pregnancy
articles.summary: When to start pregnancy check-ups, how many to have, and what happens at them.
body: Antenatal care means the check-ups a woman has with a midwife or other trained health worker while she is pregnant. These visits help keep mother and baby healthy.

The World Health Organization recommends that the first check-up happens in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, and that a pregnant woman has at least eight contacts in total. After the first, contacts are suggested at about 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks.

At these visits health workers can talk with you about healthy eating and which vitamins or minerals you may need, physical activity, avoiding tobacco, alcohol and drugs, and preventing malaria and HIV. You may have blood tests, a tetanus vaccination and a scan to check on the baby.

Health workers can also help with common problems such as nausea, back pain and constipation, talk about family planning for after the birth, and support women who are experiencing violence from a partner.
keyPoints: Start check-ups in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
Aim for at least eight antenatal contacts.
Check-ups cover nutrition, malaria and HIV prevention, tests and vaccination.
whenToGetHelp: Go for your first check-up as soon as you know you are pregnant, ideally in the first 12 weeks.
If you have heavy bleeding or fits (convulsions), go to a health facility immediately.

faqs.q: When should I start antenatal care?
faqs.tags: first check up pregnancy visit clinic start ANC
faqs.a: The World Health Organization recommends your first antenatal check-up in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Go as soon as you know you are pregnant.

faqs.q: How many antenatal visits should I have?
faqs.tags: number check ups contacts pregnancy ANC eight
faqs.a: The World Health Organization recommends at least eight antenatal contacts: the first in the first 12 weeks, then at about 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks.

faqs.q: What happens at an antenatal check-up?
faqs.tags: visit test pregnancy check what happen
faqs.a: Health workers talk with you about healthy eating, vitamins and minerals, physical activity, and preventing malaria and HIV. You may have blood tests, a tetanus vaccination and a scan, and get help with problems like nausea or back pain.

faqs.q: What should I eat during pregnancy?
faqs.tags: food diet nutrition vitamins pregnant eat
faqs.a: At antenatal check-ups a health worker will advise you on healthy eating and on which vitamins or minerals you may need, such as iron and folic acid. Ask at your next visit about what is right for you.

articles.title: Staying safe in pregnancy and childbirth
articles.summary: The main dangers in pregnancy and birth, and why giving birth with a skilled health worker matters.
body: Most deaths from pregnancy and childbirth can be prevented or treated. The World Health Organization lists the main causes as severe bleeding (mostly after birth), infections (usually after birth), high blood pressure in pregnancy (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia), complications during delivery, and unsafe abortion.
Severe bleeding after birth can kill a healthy woman within hours if she is not cared for. Health workers can give treatment straight after birth that reduces this risk.
High blood pressure in pregnancy should be found and managed early, before it leads to fits (convulsions). This is one reason antenatal check-ups matter.
Having a skilled health worker with you during and after childbirth can make the difference between life and death for a woman and her newborn.
keyPoints: Most pregnancy-related deaths are preventable.
Give birth with a skilled health worker whenever possible.
Heavy bleeding and fits (convulsions) are emergencies.
whenToGetHelp: Heavy bleeding during pregnancy or after birth: go to a health facility immediately.
Fits (convulsions): get urgent help.
Feeling very unwell after giving birth: see a health worker quickly.

faqs.q: What are the danger signs in pregnancy?
faqs.tags: danger warning signs risk pregnant complication
faqs.a: The main dangers are severe bleeding, infection, high blood pressure that can lead to fits (convulsions), problems during delivery, and unsafe abortion. Heavy bleeding and fits are emergencies: go to a health facility immediately.

faqs.q: Why should I give birth with a skilled health worker?
faqs.tags: deliver birth hospital clinic midwife home skilled attendant
faqs.a: Complications can happen quickly during and after birth. Care from a skilled health worker can make the difference between life and death for the mother and the baby, for example by treating heavy bleeding straight away.

articles.title: Pregnancy in adolescent girls
articles.summary: Why pregnancy carries extra risks for girls under 20, and why care matters.
body: Pregnancy carries higher risks for adolescent girls (aged 10 to 19) than for women in their early twenties. Girls have a higher risk of eclampsia (fits linked to high blood pressure) and serious infections, and their babies are more likely to be born small or too early.

Child marriage, sexual abuse, and difficulty getting contraception all increase the chance that a girl becomes pregnant. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest rate of births to adolescent girls in the world.
A pregnant girl deserves respectful care. Going to antenatal check-ups early helps protect her and her baby.
keyPoints: Pregnancy is riskier for girls under 20.
Early antenatal care helps protect mother and baby.
No girl should be forced into marriage or sex.
whenToGetHelp: Start antenatal check-ups as early as possible.
If someone is forcing you into sex or marriage, you can ask a trusted adult or a support service for help.

faqs.q: Is pregnancy dangerous for teenage girls?
faqs.tags: teen adolescent young girl pregnant risk age
faqs.a: Pregnancy carries higher risks for girls aged 10 to 19, including fits linked to high blood pressure and serious infections, and babies are more likely to be born small or early. Early, regular antenatal check-ups help protect both mother and baby.

articles.title: Family planning and contraception
articles.summary: What family planning is, the main types of contraception, and common worries.
body: Family planning lets people choose whether and when to have children, and how many. It is done using contraception and, for couples who struggle to get pregnant, treatment for infertility.

Some methods are very effective and last a long time: implants, intrauterine devices (IUDs or coils), and sterilisation. Others work well when used correctly every time: pills, injections, patches and vaginal rings. Condoms prevent pregnancy if used correctly. Methods based on tracking fertile days, and withdrawal, are less reliable.
The methods in WHO guidelines have been tested for safety and are safe for most people. Modern contraceptives do not cause infertility.
The right method depends on your health, your needs and what you prefer. A health worker can help you choose.
Condoms are the only method that protects against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.
keyPoints: Implants and IUDs are among the most effective methods.
Modern contraceptives do not cause infertility.
Only condoms also protect against STIs and HIV.
whenToGetHelp: Talk to a health worker to choose a method that suits you.
If you have side effects that worry you, go back to a health worker rather than stopping on your own.

faqs.q: What is family planning?
faqs.a: Family planning lets people decide whether and when to have children, and how many. It uses contraception and, for couples having difficulty, infertility treatment. It also helps protect the health of women and girls.

faqs.q: What family planning methods are available?
faqs.tags: contraceptive types options pills implant injection IUD coil
faqs.a: Long-lasting, very effective methods include implants, IUDs (coils) and sterilisation. Pills, injections, patches and rings work well when used correctly. Condoms prevent pregnancy if used correctly. Counting fertile days and withdrawal are less reliable. A health worker can help you choose.

faqs.q: Which contraceptive is the most effective?
faqs.a: Implants, intrauterine devices (IUDs or coils) and sterilisation are among the most effective, long-lasting methods. Pills, injections, patches and rings also work well when used correctly every time.

faqs.q: Do contraceptives cause infertility?
faqs.tags: barren cannot get pregnant later myth side effect
faqs.a: No. The World Health Organization says modern contraceptive methods do not cause infertility.

faqs.q: Which contraceptive also protects against STIs and HIV?
faqs.a: Condoms are the only contraceptive method that protects against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.

articles.title: Protecting yourself during sex
articles.summary: How condoms, testing and vaccines help protect your sexual health.
body: Condoms, used correctly and every time, are one of the most effective ways to protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. Use them for vaginal, oral and anal sex when possible.
Condoms do not fully protect against infections that cause sores outside the area they cover, such as syphilis and genital herpes.
Testing for HIV and other STIs, and treating sexual partners, help stop infections from spreading. Vaccines are available against two infections spread by sex: hepatitis B and HPV.
Many STIs cause no symptoms, so you can have one without knowing. Getting tested is the only way to be sure.
keyPoints: Use a condom correctly every time you have sex.
Many STIs have no symptoms — testing is the only way to know.
Vaccines protect against hepatitis B and HPV.
whenToGetHelp: If you notice anything unusual in your genital area or are worried about an infection, see a health worker.
If you had sex without a condom and are worried about HIV, ask a health worker quickly about testing and prevention medicine (PEP).

faqs.q: How can I protect myself during sex?
faqs.a: Use a condom correctly every time you have sex. Get tested for HIV and other STIs, and make sure partners are tested and treated too. Vaccines protect against hepatitis B and HPV.

faqs.q: Do condoms protect against all STIs?
faqs.a: Condoms used correctly every time are one of the best protections against STIs, including HIV. But they do not fully protect against infections that cause sores outside the area they cover, such as syphilis and genital herpes.

articles.title: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
articles.summary: How STIs spread, why many have no symptoms, and which can be cured.
body: More than 30 kinds of bacteria, viruses and parasites can be passed on through vaginal, anal or oral sex. Some STIs can also pass from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.
STIs often cause no symptoms. More than 1 million curable STIs are caught every day around the world, and most of them have no symptoms.
Four common STIs can be cured with medicine: syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis. Infections caused by viruses, such as herpes and HIV, cannot be cured, but medicines can control them.

Untreated STIs can cause serious problems, including infertility in women, problems in pregnancy, stillbirth and harm to newborn babies. They can also increase the risk of getting HIV. Pregnant women are among the groups for whom STI testing is especially important.
keyPoints: Many STIs have no symptoms.
Syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis can be cured.
Partners need treatment too, to stop reinfection.
whenToGetHelp: If you are worried you may have an STI — many have no symptoms, so ask for a test.
If you are pregnant, ask about STI testing at your antenatal check-up.
If a partner tells you they have an STI.

faqs.q: What are STIs?
faqs.a: STIs are infections passed on through vaginal, anal or oral sex. More than 30 kinds of bacteria, viruses and parasites can spread this way, and some can also pass from mother to baby.

faqs.q: Can I have an STI without symptoms?
faqs.tags: no symptoms know if I have
faqs.a: Yes. STIs often cause no symptoms at all, so you can have one without knowing. Testing is the only way to be sure.

faqs.q: Can STIs be cured?
faqs.tags: cure treatment treatable gonorrhoea syphilis chlamydia
faqs.a: Syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis can be cured with medicine from a health worker. Herpes and HIV cannot be cured, but medicines can control them. Partners need treatment too.

faqs.q: Can an STI harm my baby?
faqs.a: Yes. Some STIs can pass to a baby during pregnancy or birth and can cause stillbirth, early birth, low birth weight or serious illness in the newborn. Ask for STI testing at your antenatal check-ups.

faqs.q: How can STIs be prevented?
faqs.a: Use condoms correctly every time you have sex, get tested, and make sure sexual partners are tested and treated. Vaccines can protect against hepatitis B and HPV.

articles.title: HIV: prevention, testing and treatment
articles.summary: How HIV spreads, how it does not, testing, treatment and protecting babies.
body: HIV is a virus that attacks the body's defence (immune) system. Without treatment it can lead to AIDS, often after many years.

HIV spreads through blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk. It can pass from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. It does not spread through kissing, hugging, shaking hands, or sharing food, water or personal objects.

You can lower your risk by using condoms, getting tested for HIV and other STIs, and using prevention medicine. PrEP is medicine taken by people without HIV to lower their risk. PEP is medicine taken soon after a possible exposure. A health worker can advise you.
Rapid tests give same-day results, and HIV self-tests exist. A positive result must be confirmed by a trained health worker. After a recent risk, a test can be repeated after 28 days.
There is no cure, but treatment (antiretroviral therapy) lets people with HIV live full and healthy lives. People on treatment whose blood shows no virus do not pass HIV to sexual partners.
Pregnant women with HIV should start treatment as soon as possible. This protects their own health and helps prevent HIV passing to the baby.
keyPoints: HIV is not spread by hugging, kissing or sharing food.
Treatment lets people with HIV live full, healthy lives.
Treatment in pregnancy helps protect the baby.
whenToGetHelp: If you think you were exposed to HIV, see a health worker as soon as possible about PEP.
If you are pregnant, ask for an HIV test at your antenatal check-up.

faqs.q: How does HIV spread?
faqs.a: HIV spreads through blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk, mainly through sex without a condom, sharing needles, and from mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Can HIV spread by hugging, kissing or sharing food?
faqs.a: No. HIV does not spread through kissing, hugging, shaking hands, or sharing food, water or personal objects.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for HIV?
faqs.a: There is no cure, but antiretroviral treatment stops the virus from multiplying. People on treatment can live full and healthy lives, and those whose blood shows no virus do not pass HIV to sexual partners.

faqs.q: Can a mother with HIV have a healthy baby?
faqs.tags: pregnant pregnancy baby mother to child
faqs.a: Yes, with treatment. Pregnant women with HIV should start antiretroviral treatment as soon as possible. It protects their health and helps prevent HIV passing to the baby. Babies of mothers with HIV should be tested early.

faqs.q: What are PrEP and PEP?
faqs.a: PrEP is medicine people without HIV can take to lower their risk of getting it. PEP is medicine taken soon after a possible exposure to HIV. A health worker can tell you if either is right for you.

faqs.q: How can I get tested for HIV?
faqs.tags: test testing know status self test
faqs.a: Health facilities offer rapid HIV tests with same-day results, and HIV self-tests also exist. A positive result must be confirmed by a trained health worker. If you had a recent risk, test again after 28 days.

articles.title: HPV and cervical cancer
articles.summary: What HPV is, how vaccination and screening protect women, and warning signs.
body: HPV (human papillomavirus) is a very common infection passed on through sex. Almost all sexually active people get it at some point, usually without symptoms, and the body usually clears it on its own.

When certain types of HPV stay in the cervix for a long time, they can cause changes in the cells that may slowly become cancer. This usually takes 15 to 20 years, but can be faster (5 to 10 years) in women whose immune system is weak, such as women with untreated HIV.
Vaccination protects against the HPV types that cause most cervical cancers. The World Health Organization's priority group is girls aged 9 to 14, before they become sexually active.

Screening finds changes before they become cancer. WHO recommends screening every 5 to 10 years from age 30, or every 3 to 5 years from age 25 for women living with HIV. Women can collect an HPV test sample themselves, and this is as reliable as a sample taken by a health worker.
Not smoking and using condoms also help reduce risk. Early cell changes can be treated with a simple procedure, and cervical cancer can be cured if found early and treated promptly.
keyPoints: HPV vaccination is recommended for girls aged 9 to 14.
Screening from age 30 (25 for women with HIV) finds changes early.
Cervical cancer can be cured if found early.
whenToGetHelp: Bleeding between periods, after sex, or after menopause.
More vaginal discharge than usual, or discharge that smells bad.
Ongoing pain in the back, legs or pelvis, swollen legs, weight loss or tiredness.

faqs.q: What is HPV?
faqs.a: HPV (human papillomavirus) is a very common infection passed on through sex. Most people get it at some point without symptoms, and the body usually clears it. Some types, if they stay for years, can cause cervical cancer.

faqs.q: How can women protect themselves from HPV and cervical cancer?
faqs.tags: prevent protect HPV cervical cancer women
faqs.a: HPV vaccination (for girls aged 9 to 14), regular screening (every 5 to 10 years from age 30, or every 3 to 5 years from 25 for women with HIV), not smoking and using condoms all help. Early cell changes found by screening can be treated.

faqs.q: Who should get the HPV vaccine?
faqs.a: The World Health Organization's priority group is girls aged 9 to 14, before they become sexually active. One or two doses are given depending on the country's schedule; people with weak immune systems, including people living with HIV, may need more.

faqs.q: When should I be screened for cervical cancer?
faqs.tags: screening test check pap HPV test age
faqs.a: WHO recommends screening with an HPV test every 5 to 10 years starting at age 30. Women living with HIV should start at 25 and screen every 3 to 5 years. Women can collect the sample themselves.

faqs.q: What are the warning signs of cervical cancer?
faqs.a: See a health worker if you have bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause, more or bad-smelling discharge, ongoing back, leg or pelvic pain, swollen legs, weight loss or tiredness. Early changes usually cause no symptoms, so screening matters.

faqs.q: Can cervical cancer be cured?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is found early and treated promptly. Early cell changes can be treated with a simple procedure before they ever become cancer.

articles.title: Care for mother and baby after birth
articles.summary: When mother and baby should be checked in the first six weeks after birth.
body: The first weeks after birth are when most deaths of mothers and newborns happen, so check-ups for both are very important.

The World Health Organization recommends care in a health facility for at least 24 hours after birth, and at least three more check-ups in the first six weeks: between 48 and 72 hours, between 7 and 14 days, and in week six. If the baby is born at home, the first check should happen as early as possible and within 24 hours.

Check-ups look for danger signs in the mother or baby, and help with common problems such as pain and swollen breasts. They include support with breastfeeding, vaccination for the baby, family planning, and checking how the mother is feeling emotionally.
Having a baby can bring a lot of stress and worry. Health workers can check for depression and anxiety after birth and help you get support.
keyPoints: Stay at least 24 hours in a health facility after birth if you can.
Three more check-ups in the first six weeks.
Your feelings matter too — ask for help if you feel low or anxious.
whenToGetHelp: Heavy bleeding or feeling very unwell after birth: go to a health facility immediately.
If your baby is not feeding well or seems unwell, get help quickly.
If you feel very sad, worried or unable to cope.

faqs.q: When should mother and baby be checked after birth?
faqs.tags: postnatal after delivery check up visit newborn
faqs.a: WHO recommends care in a health facility for at least 24 hours after birth, then at least three more check-ups: at 48–72 hours, at 7–14 days, and in week six. After a home birth, the first check should be within 24 hours.

faqs.q: What happens at a postnatal check-up?
faqs.a: Health workers look for danger signs in mother and baby, help with problems like pain and swollen breasts, support breastfeeding, vaccinate the baby, talk about family planning, and check how the mother is feeling emotionally.

faqs.q: Is it normal to feel sad or worried after having a baby?
faqs.tags: postnatal depression anxiety mood after birth feelings
faqs.a: Having a baby can bring a lot of stress and worry. Health workers can check for depression and anxiety after birth and help you get support, so tell them how you are feeling.

articles.title: Breastfeeding
articles.summary: When to start, how long to give only breastmilk, and the benefits for mother and baby.
body: WHO and UNICEF recommend starting breastfeeding within the first hour after birth.
For the first 6 months, babies should have only breastmilk — no other food or drinks, not even water. Breastfeed whenever the baby wants, day and night.
From 6 months, start giving safe, nourishing foods while continuing to breastfeed up to two years of age or longer.

Breastmilk is safe and clean, and contains antibodies that help protect babies from many common childhood illnesses. Breastfed children are less likely to become overweight or develop diabetes later in life. Women who breastfeed have a lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
keyPoints: Start within the first hour after birth.
Only breastmilk for the first 6 months — not even water.
Keep breastfeeding with other foods up to 2 years or beyond.
whenToGetHelp: If breastfeeding is painful or your breasts are very swollen, ask a health worker for help.
If your baby is not feeding well or seems unwell.

faqs.q: When should I start breastfeeding?
faqs.a: WHO and UNICEF recommend starting breastfeeding within the first hour after birth.

faqs.q: How long should I give my baby only breastmilk?
faqs.tags: exclusive breastfeeding six months water food
faqs.a: For the first 6 months, give only breastmilk — no other food or drinks, not even water. Then add safe, nourishing foods while continuing to breastfeed up to 2 years or beyond.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Breastmilk is clean and safe and contains antibodies that protect babies from common illnesses. Breastfed children are less likely to become overweight or develop diabetes later. Mothers who breastfeed have a lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer.

articles.title: Looking after your mental wellbeing
articles.summary: Common feelings and conditions in young people, what helps, and when to reach out.
body: Mental health problems are common. Around the world, about one in seven young people aged 10 to 19 has a mental health condition. Anxiety and depression are among the most common.

Anxiety can feel like panic or constant worry. Depression and anxiety can both cause sudden changes in mood. They can affect school, friendships and daily life, and pulling away from others can make loneliness worse.

Things that help protect mental health include good sleep, regular exercise, learning ways to cope with problems and manage emotions, and having supportive people at home, at school and in the community.
Shame and stigma often stop people from asking for help. Reaching out is a sign of strength. Talking to someone you trust or a health worker can help.
keyPoints: About one in seven young people has a mental health condition.
Sleep, exercise and supportive people help.
Asking for help is a sign of strength.
whenToGetHelp: If worry or sadness lasts a long time or stops you from doing daily things.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, get help now from someone you trust or the nearest health facility.

faqs.q: Is it normal to feel anxious or sad?
faqs.tags: worry stress sad down low mood feel
faqs.a: Everyone feels worried or sad sometimes. When these feelings last a long time or stop you from doing daily things, it may be anxiety or depression, which are common and can be helped. Talk to someone you trust or a health worker.

faqs.q: What can help my mental wellbeing?
faqs.tags: cope coping stress better mental health tips
faqs.a: Good sleep, regular exercise, learning ways to cope with problems and manage emotions, and spending time with supportive people all help protect mental health.

faqs.q: Where can I get help for my mental health?
faqs.a: Start by talking to someone you trust, such as a family member, teacher or friend, or a health worker. Asking for help is a sign of strength. If you ever think about harming yourself, get help immediately.

articles.title: Emergency contraception
articles.summary: What to do after sex without protection, or if a condom broke or a pill was missed.
body: Emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy after sex without contraception, if contraception failed (for example a condom broke or slipped, or pills were missed), or after sexual assault.
The World Health Organization recommends using it within 5 days (120 hours) of unprotected sex. It works better the sooner it is used.

There are emergency contraceptive pills and the copper IUD (coil). The copper IUD is the most effective emergency method, but it is not fitted after sexual assault because of the higher risk of infection.

Any woman or girl of reproductive age can use emergency contraception — there are no age limits. It is not an abortion: it works by preventing or delaying the release of an egg, and it cannot end a pregnancy that has already started or harm a developing baby.

Side effects such as nausea, tiredness or a little irregular bleeding are usually mild and pass on their own. Emergency contraception does not harm future fertility. If you need it often, a health worker can help you choose a regular method.
keyPoints: Use within 5 days of unprotected sex — the sooner the better.
It does not cause abortion and does not harm future fertility.
There is no age limit.
whenToGetHelp: Go to a health worker or health facility as soon as possible after unprotected sex.
After sexual assault, a health facility can also offer other care and support.

faqs.q: What is emergency contraception?
faqs.a: Emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy after sex without protection, if a condom broke or pills were missed, or after sexual assault. It comes as pills or a copper IUD (coil).

faqs.q: How soon after sex do I need emergency contraception?
faqs.tags: morning after pill time days hours late
faqs.a: WHO recommends using emergency contraception within 5 days (120 hours) of unprotected sex. It works better the sooner it is used, so go to a health worker as soon as you can.

faqs.q: Does emergency contraception cause abortion?
faqs.tags: morning after pill abortion pregnancy harm baby
faqs.a: No. Emergency contraception prevents or delays the release of an egg. It cannot end a pregnancy that has already started and it does not harm a developing baby.

faqs.q: Can emergency contraception make me infertile?
faqs.tags: morning after pill future fertility side effects
faqs.a: No. WHO says emergency contraception does not harm future fertility. Side effects such as nausea or slight irregular bleeding are usually mild and pass on their own.

faqs.q: Can a young girl use emergency contraception?
faqs.tags: teen age limit adolescent girl morning after
faqs.a: Yes. WHO says any woman or girl of reproductive age can use emergency contraception, and there are no age limits.

articles.title: Managing your period with dignity
articles.summary: Why menstrual health matters, and what girls and women need to manage their periods well.
body: About 1.8 billion people around the world have a period every month. Periods are natural, but many girls and women cannot manage them in a healthy and dignified way.

Stigma, teasing, cultural taboos, poverty, and a lack of toilets, water and period products can make periods hard. This can cause stress and worry, and can stop girls from going to school or taking part in community life.
UNICEF says four things help: support from the people around you, knowledge and skills about periods, safe toilets and washing facilities, and access to pads or other absorbent materials.
There is nothing shameful about having a period. Talking openly helps girls feel confident and safe.
keyPoints: Periods are natural and nothing to be ashamed of.
Girls need support, knowledge, facilities and period products.
No girl should have to miss school because of her period.
whenToGetHelp: If you have no safe way to manage your period, talk to a trusted adult, teacher or health worker.
If your periods are very painful or very heavy, see a health worker.

faqs.q: Why do some girls miss school during their period?
faqs.tags: school period stigma pads toilets miss class
faqs.a: UNICEF says stigma, teasing, a lack of toilets, water and period products, and poverty can stop girls from going to school during their period. Support, knowledge, safe facilities and access to pads help girls stay in school.

faqs.q: Is it shameful to have a period?
faqs.a: No. Periods are a natural part of life for about 1.8 billion people every month. There is nothing shameful about them, and talking openly helps girls feel confident and safe.

articles.title: Endometriosis
articles.summary: A common condition that can cause very painful periods and long-lasting pelvic pain.
body: Endometriosis is a long-lasting condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows outside the womb. It causes inflammation and scar tissue.

It affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age around the world. Symptoms can include severe pain during periods, heavy periods, pelvic pain that continues after the period ends, bloating and nausea, and difficulty getting pregnant. It can also cause pain during sex, when passing urine or stools, and can affect mental health. Some women have no symptoms.
Because symptoms vary, endometriosis is often found late — on average 4 to 12 years after symptoms start.

There is no cure, but medicines (including pain relief and hormonal treatments), surgery for some women, physiotherapy and talking therapies can reduce pain and improve daily life. Fertility treatment may help women who want to become pregnant.
keyPoints: About 1 in 10 women have endometriosis.
Severe period pain is not something you just have to live with.
Treatment can control symptoms, even though there is no cure.
whenToGetHelp: Talk to a health worker about period pain that is severe or that stops your daily life.
Tell a health worker if you have pelvic pain that does not go away when your period ends.

faqs.q: What is endometriosis?
faqs.a: Endometriosis is a long-lasting condition where tissue like the lining of the womb grows outside the womb, causing inflammation and scarring. It affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age.

faqs.q: What are the symptoms of endometriosis?
faqs.tags: endometriosis signs severe period pain pelvic
faqs.a: Symptoms can include severe period pain, heavy periods, pelvic pain that continues after your period, bloating, nausea, pain during sex, and difficulty getting pregnant. Some women have no symptoms.

faqs.q: Can endometriosis be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure, but treatment helps. Medicines, surgery for some women, physiotherapy and talking therapies can reduce pain and improve daily life. A health worker can explain the options.

articles.title: Vaginal discharge: what is normal
articles.summary: What healthy discharge looks like, signs of infection, and how to care for the area.
body: Vaginal discharge is normal and most women and girls have it. It keeps the vagina clean and moist and helps protect it from infection.

Normal discharge has no strong or unpleasant smell and can be clear or white, thick and sticky, or slippery and wet. There may be more during pregnancy, when you are sexually active, when using contraception, and around the middle of your cycle.

A change in smell, colour or texture can be a sign of infection. A fishy smell can mean bacterial vaginosis; thick white discharge like cottage cheese can mean thrush; green, yellow or frothy discharge can mean trichomoniasis; and discharge with pelvic pain, bleeding, blisters or sores can be a sign of a sexually transmitted infection.

To avoid irritation, wash the skin around the vagina gently with water and mild, unperfumed soap. Do not use perfumed soaps, scented wipes or deodorants there, and do not wash inside the vagina (douching).
keyPoints: Discharge is normal and protects the vagina.
Do not wash inside the vagina.
A change in smell, colour or texture should be checked.
whenToGetHelp: Discharge that changes colour, smell or texture, or there is much more than usual.
Itching or soreness, pain when you pass urine, or pelvic pain.
Bleeding between periods or after sex.

faqs.q: Is vaginal discharge normal?
faqs.a: Yes. Most women and girls have discharge. It keeps the vagina clean and moist and helps protect it from infection. Normal discharge is clear or white and has no strong or unpleasant smell.

faqs.q: When is vaginal discharge a sign of infection?
faqs.tags: discharge smell colour green yellow fishy itching infection
faqs.a: See a health worker if discharge changes colour, smell or texture, if there is much more than usual, or if you have itching, soreness, pain when passing urine, pelvic pain, or bleeding between periods or after sex. Do not try to diagnose it yourself.

faqs.q: How should I clean my private parts?
faqs.tags: wash clean hygiene vagina soap douche
faqs.a: Wash the skin around the vagina gently with water and mild, unperfumed soap. Do not use perfumed soaps, scented wipes or deodorants there, and do not wash inside the vagina, because it cleans itself.

articles.title: Malaria and pregnancy
articles.summary: Why malaria is especially dangerous in pregnancy and how to protect yourself.
body: Malaria is spread by the bites of infected mosquitoes. It is a serious disease, but it can be prevented and cured. Africa carries about 95% of the world's malaria cases and deaths.
Pregnant women and girls, babies and young children are at higher risk of severe malaria. Malaria in pregnancy can cause a baby to be born too early or too small.

Protect yourself by sleeping under an insecticide-treated mosquito net, and by using repellent, protective clothing and window screens where you can. In pregnancy, health workers may offer preventive malaria treatment at antenatal check-ups.
Early signs are fever, headache and chills, usually 10 to 15 days after a bite. Malaria can become severe very quickly, so a suspected case should be tested and treated straight away.
keyPoints: Sleep under a treated mosquito net every night.
Ask about preventive malaria treatment at antenatal check-ups.
Fever in pregnancy needs a malaria test straight away.
whenToGetHelp: Fever, headache or chills: get tested for malaria at a health facility the same day.
Extreme tiredness, confusion, fits (convulsions), difficulty breathing, dark urine, yellow eyes or unusual bleeding are emergencies.

faqs.q: Is malaria dangerous in pregnancy?
faqs.tags: malaria pregnant pregnancy baby risk harm affect unborn
faqs.a: Yes. Pregnant women are at higher risk of severe malaria, and malaria in pregnancy can cause a baby to be born too early or too small. Sleep under a treated net and ask about preventive treatment at antenatal check-ups.

faqs.q: How can I prevent malaria?
faqs.a: Sleep under an insecticide-treated mosquito net, and use repellent, protective clothing and window screens where you can. Pregnant women can ask about preventive malaria treatment at antenatal check-ups.

faqs.q: What are the signs of malaria?
faqs.a: Early signs are fever, headache and chills. Severe signs include extreme tiredness, confusion, fits, difficulty breathing, dark urine, yellow eyes and unusual bleeding. Malaria can become severe quickly, so get tested and treated straight away.

articles.title: Caring for your newborn baby
articles.summary: Essential care in the first weeks, and the danger signs that need help fast.
body: The first month is the most dangerous time of a baby's life, and three-quarters of newborn deaths happen in the first week. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest rate of newborn deaths in the world. Many can be prevented with simple care.

Every baby needs: to be kept warm, especially with skin-to-skin contact with the mother; clean care of the umbilical cord and skin; early and exclusive breastfeeding; a check for health problems; and preventive care such as vaccines.
Families should register the birth, bring the baby for vaccinations on time, and go to the postnatal check-ups. Staying at the health facility for 24 hours after birth is recommended.
Babies born early or small need extra care: skin-to-skin warmth, help with breastfeeding, careful hand-washing and close watching for danger signs.
keyPoints: Keep your baby warm with skin-to-skin contact.
Breastfeed early and give only breastmilk.
Know the danger signs and act fast.
whenToGetHelp: The baby is not feeding well or stops feeding.
The baby is less active than usual, has difficulty breathing, has a fever or feels cold.
The baby has fits (convulsions). Go to a health facility immediately.

faqs.q: What are the danger signs in a newborn baby?
faqs.tags: newborn baby danger signs sick infant
faqs.a: Get help fast if your baby has feeding problems, is less active than usual, has difficulty breathing, has a fever or feels cold, or has fits (convulsions).

faqs.q: How do I care for my newborn baby?
faqs.tags: newborn care baby warm cord breastfeed
faqs.a: Keep your baby warm with skin-to-skin contact, keep the umbilical cord and skin clean, breastfeed early and give only breastmilk, go to postnatal check-ups and get vaccinations on time.

faqs.q: How do I keep my newborn warm?
faqs.tags: baby cold warm skin to skin
faqs.a: Skin-to-skin contact between mother and baby is one of the best ways to keep a newborn warm. Babies born early or small especially need this warmth.

articles.title: Anaemia (low blood)
articles.summary: Why anaemia is common in women and girls, its signs, and how to prevent it.
body: Anaemia means there are too few red blood cells or too little haemoglobin, so the body does not get enough oxygen. It is very common in women and girls — about 3 in 10 women and nearly 4 in 10 pregnant women worldwide — and Africa is among the most affected regions.
Common signs are tiredness, dizziness, cold hands and feet, headache and shortness of breath when active. Severe anaemia can cause pale skin and nails and a fast heartbeat.

Causes include lack of iron and other nutrients, blood loss from heavy periods or childbirth, and infections such as malaria and worms. In pregnancy, anaemia is linked to babies born early or small and to deaths of mothers.

To help prevent it: eat iron-rich foods such as fish, meat, poultry, beans and dark green leafy vegetables, together with foods rich in vitamin C; avoid tea and coffee with iron-rich meals; prevent and treat malaria and worms; wash hands with soap and use clean toilets; space pregnancies at least 2 years apart; and get heavy periods treated. Take supplements only if a health worker recommends them.
keyPoints: Anaemia is very common in women and pregnant women.
Eat iron-rich foods with vitamin C.
Prevent malaria and treat heavy periods.
whenToGetHelp: If you often feel very tired, dizzy or short of breath.
If you are pregnant, ask about anaemia checks at antenatal care.
If your periods are very heavy.

faqs.q: What is anaemia?
faqs.a: Anaemia means there are too few red blood cells or too little haemoglobin, so the body gets less oxygen. It is very common in women, girls and pregnant women.

faqs.q: What are the signs of anaemia?
faqs.tags: anaemia anemia symptoms tired dizzy weak
faqs.a: Common signs are tiredness, dizziness, cold hands and feet, headache and shortness of breath when active. Severe anaemia can cause pale skin and nails and a fast heartbeat.

faqs.q: How can I prevent anaemia?
faqs.a: Eat iron-rich foods such as fish, meat, beans and dark green leafy vegetables with vitamin C-rich foods, avoid tea and coffee with those meals, prevent malaria and worms, space pregnancies at least 2 years apart, and get heavy periods treated. Take supplements only if a health worker recommends them.

faqs.q: What foods are rich in iron?
faqs.a: WHO lists lean red meat, fish, poultry, beans and other legumes, fortified cereals and dark green leafy vegetables. Eating vitamin C-rich foods at the same meal helps the body absorb the iron.

articles.title: Urinary tract infections (UTIs)
articles.summary: Common signs of a bladder infection and simple ways to help prevent it.
body: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection of the bladder, urethra or kidneys, usually caused by bacteria from the bowel. Women get UTIs more easily than men because their urethra is shorter.

Signs include pain or burning when passing urine, needing to pass urine more often or more urgently, cloudy or bloody urine, lower tummy pain or pain in the back just under the ribs, fever or shivering, and feeling tired or weak.

Rest and drinking enough fluids can help. To help prevent UTIs: wipe from front to back after using the toilet, keep the area clean and dry, drink plenty of water, pass urine soon after sex, wear cotton underwear, do not hold in urine, and avoid scented soaps in the genital area.
A kidney infection can be serious if it is not treated.
keyPoints: Wipe from front to back.
Drink plenty of water and do not hold in urine.
Pass urine soon after sex.
whenToGetHelp: If you are pregnant and have signs of a UTI, see a health worker quickly.
Fever or shivering, pain in the back under the ribs, or blood in your urine.
Symptoms that get worse quickly or keep coming back.
Confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking: go to a health facility immediately.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a urinary tract infection?
faqs.tags: UTI bladder infection burning pee urine pain
faqs.a: Signs include pain or burning when passing urine, needing to go more often or urgently, cloudy or bloody urine, lower tummy pain or back pain under the ribs, fever or shivering, and feeling tired or weak.

faqs.q: How can I prevent a UTI?
faqs.a: Wipe from front to back, keep the area clean and dry, drink plenty of water, pass urine soon after sex, wear cotton underwear, do not hold in urine, and avoid scented soaps in the genital area.

faqs.q: When is a UTI serious?
faqs.a: See a health worker quickly if you are pregnant, have a fever or shivering, pain in the back under the ribs, blood in your urine, or symptoms that get worse or keep coming back. Confusion or drowsiness is an emergency.

articles.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
articles.summary: A common hormone condition that can cause irregular periods, extra hair and difficulty getting pregnant.
body: PCOS is a common hormone condition, affecting about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age. Up to 70% of women with PCOS do not know they have it.

Signs can include irregular, absent or sometimes heavy periods; difficulty getting pregnant; extra hair on the face or body; thinning hair on the head; and acne or oily skin. It is a leading cause of infertility.
PCOS can raise the risk of diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and problems in pregnancy. It can also affect self-esteem and mood.

There is no cure, but treatment can help with periods, skin and hair, and fertility, and can lower long-term health risks. Healthy eating and physical activity help all women with PCOS, even without weight loss.
keyPoints: About 1 in 10 women have PCOS — most don't know it.
Irregular periods and extra hair are common signs.
Treatment and healthy habits help, even without a cure.
whenToGetHelp: Talk to a health worker if your periods are irregular or absent, or if you have trouble getting pregnant.

faqs.q: What is PCOS?
faqs.a: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormone condition affecting about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age. Most women with PCOS don't know they have it.

faqs.q: What are the signs of PCOS?
faqs.tags: PCOS symptoms irregular periods hair acne
faqs.a: Signs can include irregular or absent periods, difficulty getting pregnant, extra hair on the face or body, thinning hair on the head, and acne or oily skin.

faqs.q: Can a woman with PCOS get pregnant?
faqs.a: Yes, many can, with support. PCOS is a leading cause of infertility, but lifestyle changes and fertility treatments can help. Pregnancies may need extra check-ups.

articles.title: Difficulty getting pregnant (infertility)
articles.summary: What infertility is, its causes in both women and men, and how it can often be prevented.
body: Infertility means not becoming pregnant after 12 months or more of regular sex without contraception. About 1 in 6 people experience it during their lives.
Infertility can be caused by problems in the man, the woman, or both — and sometimes no cause is found. Yet women are often blamed, and many face stigma, violence or divorce because of it.

In women, causes include blocked fallopian tubes (often from untreated STIs, unsafe abortion, or infection after childbirth), conditions of the womb such as fibroids or endometriosis, and PCOS. In men, causes include blockages from injury or infection, hormone problems, and problems with sperm. Smoking, heavy drinking and obesity can affect both.

Infertility can often be prevented: by preventing and treating STIs early, by avoiding unsafe abortion and infections after childbirth, and by healthy habits. Contraception does not cause infertility.
keyPoints: Men can be the cause as often as women.
Untreated STIs are a preventable cause.
Contraception does not cause infertility.
whenToGetHelp: If you have not become pregnant after 12 months of regular sex without contraception, a couple can talk to a health worker together.

faqs.q: What is infertility?
faqs.a: Infertility means not becoming pregnant after 12 months or more of regular sex without contraception. About 1 in 6 people experience it during their lives.

faqs.q: Is infertility always the woman's fault?
faqs.tags: infertility man woman blame husband cause
faqs.a: No. Infertility can be caused by the man, the woman, or both, and sometimes no cause is found. Blaming women is unfair and harmful.

faqs.q: How can infertility be prevented?
faqs.a: Many causes can be prevented: get STIs tested and treated early, avoid unsafe abortion and infection after childbirth, and avoid smoking and heavy drinking.

articles.title: Breast health and breast cancer
articles.summary: Know the changes to look for, and why seeing a health worker early matters.
body: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women. Being a woman and getting older (over 40) are the biggest risk factors; most women who get it have no family history. Other risks include obesity, harmful alcohol use and tobacco.

Know how your breasts normally look and feel. Signs to check include a lump or thickening (often painless), a change in size or shape, dimpling, redness or other skin changes, changes to the nipple, and bloody or unusual fluid from the nipple.
Most breast lumps are not cancer. But any lump should be checked by a health worker, even if it does not hurt.
Treatment works best when cancer is found early and the full treatment is completed.
keyPoints: Most breast lumps are not cancer — but get every lump checked.
Painless lumps still need checking.
Early treatment works best.
whenToGetHelp: A new lump or thickening in the breast or armpit.
Changes in breast shape, skin, or nipple, or fluid from the nipple.
A breast wound that does not heal.

faqs.q: What are the signs of breast cancer?
faqs.a: Signs include a lump or thickening (often painless), a change in breast size or shape, dimpling or redness of the skin, changes to the nipple, and bloody or unusual fluid from the nipple. See a health worker about any of these.

faqs.q: Is every breast lump cancer?
faqs.a: No — most breast lumps are not cancer. But every lump should be checked by a health worker, even if it does not hurt.

articles.title: Menopause
articles.summary: When periods stop for good, common symptoms, and health after menopause.
body: Menopause is when monthly periods stop for good because the ovaries stop releasing eggs. It is confirmed after 12 months in a row without a period. Most women reach menopause between ages 45 and 55.

The years before (perimenopause) can bring changes in periods, hot flushes and night sweats, vaginal dryness and pain during sex, leaking urine, trouble sleeping, and mood changes. Some women have few symptoms; others have symptoms that affect daily life.
Pregnancy is still possible until periods have stopped for 12 months, so keep using contraception until then. STIs, including HIV, can still be caught after menopause.
After menopause, bones get weaker and the risk of heart disease rises. Treatments are available for symptoms. Talk to a health worker — there is no need to feel embarrassed.
keyPoints: Menopause usually happens between 45 and 55.
Use contraception until 12 months without a period.
Treatments can ease symptoms — ask a health worker.
whenToGetHelp: If symptoms affect your health or daily life.
Any bleeding after your periods have stopped for good should be checked.

faqs.q: What is menopause?
faqs.tags: menopause periods stop change of life when start age
faqs.a: Menopause is when monthly periods stop for good because the ovaries stop releasing eggs. It is confirmed after 12 months in a row without a period, and usually happens between ages 45 and 55.

faqs.q: What are the symptoms of menopause?
faqs.a: Symptoms can include changes in periods, hot flushes and night sweats, vaginal dryness and pain during sex, leaking urine, trouble sleeping, and mood changes. Treatments can help — talk to a health worker.

faqs.q: Can I get pregnant during menopause?
faqs.a: Pregnancy is still possible until your periods have stopped for 12 months in a row, so keep using contraception until then.

articles.title: Violence against women
articles.summary: What violence includes, how it harms health, and that support is available.
body: Violence against women includes physical, sexual and emotional harm, threats and controlling behaviour — by a partner, an ex-partner or anyone else. About 1 in 3 women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence. In sub-Saharan Africa, about 1 in 3 women have experienced violence from a partner.

Violence harms health: injuries, pain, unwanted pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections including HIV, problems in pregnancy, and depression, anxiety and trouble sleeping. It also harms children who live with it.
Violence is never the victim's fault. Health services can offer care, including sexual and reproductive health care and mental health support, and can connect survivors with other services.
keyPoints: Violence is never your fault.
It includes physical, sexual and emotional abuse and control.
Health services can help survivors.
whenToGetHelp: If you are hurt, a health facility can give you care.
If you are in danger, get to a safe place and reach out to someone you trust or a support service.

faqs.q: What counts as violence against women?
faqs.a: It includes physical, sexual and emotional harm, threats, and controlling behaviour by a partner, an ex-partner or anyone else. About 1 in 3 women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence. It is never the woman's fault.

faqs.q: How does violence affect a woman's health?
faqs.a: It can cause injuries, pain, unwanted pregnancy, STIs including HIV, problems in pregnancy, and depression, anxiety and trouble sleeping. Health services can offer care and support.

articles.title: Female genital mutilation (FGM)
articles.summary: What FGM is, why it has no health benefits, and the harm it causes.
body: Female genital mutilation (FGM) means cutting or injuring a girl's or woman's genitals for non-medical reasons. It is mostly done to girls between infancy and adolescence.
FGM has no health benefits. It can cause severe pain, heavy bleeding, infection, problems passing urine, shock and even death.
Long-term, it can cause infections, painful periods and sex, scarring, mental distress, and serious problems during childbirth for both mother and baby.

FGM is recognised internationally as a violation of the human rights of girls and women. WHO strongly urges health workers never to perform it — having it done by a health worker does not make it safe. Women who have had FGM can get care for its effects.
keyPoints: FGM has no health benefits.
It can cause lifelong harm, including in childbirth.
It is a violation of girls' and women's rights.
whenToGetHelp: If a girl is at risk of FGM, reach out to a trusted adult, health worker or support service.
Women who have had FGM can ask a health worker for care, especially during pregnancy.

faqs.q: What is female genital mutilation?
faqs.a: Female genital mutilation (FGM) means cutting or injuring a girl's or woman's genitals for non-medical reasons. It has no health benefits and is a violation of the human rights of girls and women.

faqs.q: What are the health effects of FGM?
faqs.a: FGM can cause severe pain, heavy bleeding, infection, shock and death at the time. Long-term, it can cause infections, painful periods and sex, scarring, mental distress, and serious problems during childbirth.

faqs.q: Is FGM safe if a health worker does it?
faqs.a: No. WHO strongly urges health workers never to perform FGM. It has no health benefits however it is done.
